extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent agents/attorneys and patent bar exam candidates (WYSEBRIDGE review audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on post-issuance remedies for patents — when and how to use Certificates of Correction, Reissue, Reexamination, and Disclaimers, and the legal/technical requirements and limits for each procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard/threshold for permitting corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrections are allowed only when (1) the error was unintentional/unavoidable and (2) the correction is made without deceptive intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cannot make a change simply because you 'changed your mind'. This unintentional/no-deceptive-intent threshold applies across correction mechanisms (e.g., reissue oath/declaration must state reasons and lack of deceptive intent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Four available post-issuance remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Four ways to fix a patent after it issues: (1) Certificate of Correction, (2) Reissue, (3) Reexamination, (4) Disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the remedy based on the nature and severity of the error: CoC for minor clerical errors; reissue for major/substantive errors; reexamination to challenge/clarify patentability with third-party or owner-initiated art; disclaimer to give up scope/term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of Correction — proper scope (minor/non-substantive errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: For small, minor, non-'substance' issues such as spelling errors, typos, and other non-substantive printing/clerical errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'minor' error is one that doesn’t affect the scope or meaning of a patent. Cannot be used to introduce new matter or to effect changes requiring substantive reexamination. Correction is retroactive and becomes part of the patent as of the original issue date (see 35 U.S.C. 255).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of Correction — PTO vs applicant mistake and fees
rubrics_metrics.description: If the mistake is a PTO error, CoC is free (37 CFR 1.322); if the mistake is the applicant's, a fee is required (37 CFR 1.323).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small-entity discount rules may apply to applicant-paid CoC fees. Distinguish whether the error was caused by the Office or the applicant when filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of Correction — inventorship correction (consent or court order)
rubrics_metrics.description: CoC can be used to correct inventorship when all parties/inventors agree; post-AIA 37 CFR 1.324 requires either (a) statements from each added inventor, current inventors, and assignees (no deceptive intent), or (b) a court order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not all inventors agree or an inventor cannot be located, reissue should be used instead. Ensure required signed statements and assignee consents are collected before seeking CoC for inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of Correction — perfecting foreign priority (limited conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A CoC under 35 U.S.C. 255 and 37 CFR 1.323 may be requested and issued to perfect a claim for foreign priority if (1) the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) or (f) had been satisfied in the patented or parent application prior to issuance, and (2) the requirements of 37 CFR 1.55 are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If those requirements were not satisfied prior to issuance, reissue may be required instead. See MPEP 216 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on CoC for 35 U.S.C. 119(e) provisional priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications filed on or after November 29, 2000: cannot use CoC to correct a 119(e) (provisional) priority error after a patent has been granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reissue or other appropriate mechanism when provisional priority was not properly claimed and the filing date is on/after the cutoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue — general purpose and who may file
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue is used to correct major, substantive errors in an issued patent; only the patent owner(s) (not a licensee) may file a reissue application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a reissue effectively states the patent is wholly or partly defective and the owner offers to surrender the original patent; reissue is examined like a new application so new prior art may be raised and there is risk of losing the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue — requirement to identify an error and lack of deceptive intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue request must specify at least one error in detail and must be made without deceptive intent (oath/declaration must state reasons why patent is wholly or partly inoperative or invalid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to assert a non-deceptive error in the oath/declaration can defeat the reissue. Forms and paragraphs in MPEP (e.g., 1414) must be followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue — prohibition on new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue cannot add new matter; new claims must be based on the same disclosure as the original patent (no new matter allowed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissue cannot be used to introduce subject matter not originally disclosed (so no CIP-type additions). Conforming drawings to the specification is allowed; adding entirely new drawings is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue — broadening claims (time limit and conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadening reissue (new claims broader than original) may be filed but only within two years of the original patent issue date; new claims must be based on the same disclosure (no new matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All inventors and relevant parties must agree; cannot broaden to reclaim subject matter given up during original prosecution (recapture doctrine). If any aspect of a claim is broadened, the claim is considered broadened. Oath by inventors required if broadening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue — narrowing and same-scope reissue types
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrowing reissue is used to overcome newly-discovered prior art and has no time limit; same-scope reissue adds claims of the same scope (often to avoid indefiniteness errors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrowing reissue functions similarly to a statutory disclaimer with no two-year limit. Same-scope claims are often used to fix claim clarity issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue — interference-related reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: A reissue may include new claims intended to revoke or resolve an interference; such claims can be copying claims from another issued patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this type when interference procedures are implicated; ensure the new claims still meet reissue/no-new-matter constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue — things reissue can correct (inventorship, priority, disclosure flaws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue can correct: errors curable by amendment during prosecution or by filing a continuation; errors not correctible through CoC or Disclaimer; inaccurate disclosure (can conform drawings/specification but not add new drawings); inventorship errors when consent is lacking; priority errors not curable by CoC (e.g., failure to perfect priority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some priority failures (e.g., failing to claim 119(e) provisional or missing a divisional deadline) may not be curable by reissue—check specific exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue — things reissue cannot do (recapture, terminal disclaimer, best mode)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cannot add new matter; cannot recapture subject matter intentionally given up during original prosecution (recapture doctrine); cannot undo a terminal disclaimer; cannot fix best mode errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reissue introduces claims the examiner deems to claim a distinct invention, a restriction requirement may be imposed on those new claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue — required application contents, format, and amendments rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue filing must include a copy of the specification, claims, and drawings (new copies of all drawings required), double-column format on single-sided sheets, copies of any disclaimers/CoC/reexamination certificates if available, and disclosure of related proceedings; amendments in reissue must be non-cumulative and show all changes from the original every time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use strikethrough or double square brackets to show deletions; explain new claims; show status of all claims (pending/cancelled); amended/new drawings must be on a separate sheet in red ink labeled 'amended', 'new', or 'cancelled'; new claims receive next available claim numbers and old numbers must not be reassigned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue — procedural formalities (consents, IDS, oath, fees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue requires consent of all assignees (37 CFR 1.63), an offer to surrender the original patent, reassertion of foreign priority if applicable, a new Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) (duty of disclosure still applies), an oath/declaration by inventors (required if broadening) or assignee, and payment of the filing fee (small-entity discount available).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reissue is examined like a new application, file an early IDS; include copies of any related proceedings and documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution of reissue — examination, public notice, third-party actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue is examined like a new application: the file is open to public inspection; notice of reissue filing is published in the Official Gazette; reissue is examined (typically ~2 months later); third parties can file a protest within 2 months of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissue receives expedited/ex special status but opens the patent to renewed prior art scrutiny and possible abandonment; early, complete IDS is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervening rights for reissued claims
rubrics_metrics.description: No infringement by others during the period between original patent issue and reissue date for newly added claims; after the reissue date, infringement exists under the reissued claims, but courts may fashion equitable remedies for parties who made substantial preparations before reissue grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may allow continued use of already-made products but block future production; be aware of potential equitable defenses for alleged infringers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue vs Reexamination — key distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue: only patent owner may file; any prior art may be cited; reissue can broaden within 2 years; reissue requires a mistake to initiate; no automatic extensions. Reexamination: anyone can file; limited to patents and printed publications as prior art; cannot broaden claims; no mistake required; automatic extensions may apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select reissue if fixing owner-identified substantive errors or inventorship/priority problems; use reexamination for art-based challenges to patentability where broadening is not sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction requirement and divisional issues in reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: If an original file had a restriction requirement and the applicant failed to timely file a divisional after election (i.e., failed to preserve elected but not prosecuted claims), that failure generally cannot be corrected in reissue (claims become dedicated to the public). However, if two inventions were disclosed but only one was claimed (no RR was based on claims), reissue may be used to add claims to the second invention and then a divisional reissue may be filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the original prosecution included an RR and whether any rights were lost by failing to file a divisional; reissue can sometimes be used to recover unclaimed disclosed subject matter but not claims lost by election/restriction practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miscellaneous reissue rules (continuations, design-to-utility prohibition, term)
rubrics_metrics.description: You can file a continuation in a reissue with a new oath specifying the remaining error to be fixed (but no continuation of a reexamination). Cannot use reissue to convert a design patent to a utility patent. Term and maintenance fee due dates for a reissued patent remain the same as for the original patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan prosecution strategy with term/maintenance implications in mind; reissue does not extend patent term or change maintenance schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments and claim numbering in reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments in reissue are non-cumulative and must show all changes from the original each time; when adding new claims, assign the next claim number available — do not reassign original claim numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow reissue-formatting rules for clarity and examiner processing; preserve an audit trail of all changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer — nature, who may disclaim, and formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclaimer is a way for the patent owner to give back to the public a portion of the patent's protection by disclaiming one or more claims (statutory disclaimer) or giving up patent term (terminal disclaimer). Only the owner (or part-owner) may disclaim; it must be in writing, recorded at the PTO, and a fee must be paid; must be done without deceptive intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statutory disclaimers when a claim is invalid or defective; use terminal disclaimers to overcome certain rejections (but they give up term). Terminal disclaimers in applications are revocable before patent issue (or before reexamination certificate issues), but disclaimers are otherwise irrevocable and binding on successors-in-interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer — effect on continuations and successors
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminal disclaimers do not carry over to continuations unless explicitly stated, but they do carry over to CPA and RCEs. Disclaimers are irrevocable and binding on successors-in-interest (with narrow exceptions for pre-issuance revocation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully draft any terminal disclaimer language and understand downstream effects on continuations and related applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer — inventor-specific limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each joint inventor can only disclaim his/her portion of the patent (i.e., a co-inventor cannot disclaim another inventor's share).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure proper signatures/authority when seeking partial disclaimers in jointly-owned patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer — effect on prior art and enforceability
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclaimer affects the patentee's exclusionary rights but does not change how the patent is considered for prior art purposes; disclaiming does not alter the patent's use as prior art against others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclaiming narrows enforceable rights but does not retroactively change the patent's status as prior art for invalidity analyses.
